```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the numbers behind this chapter: nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting, participation, draft picks and contracts)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- play-by-play, 2016-2025
_cols = ["game_id", "play_id", "season", "season_type", "week", "posteam", "defteam", "down", "ydstogo",
         "yardline_100", "play_type", "qb_dropback", "qb_kneel", "qb_scramble", "two_point_attempt",
         "first_down", "touchdown", "epa", "sack", "rushing_yards", "rusher_player_name",
         "fourth_down_converted"]
ALL = pbp(list(range(2016, 2026)), columns=_cols)
REG = ALL[ALL["season_type"] == "REG"]
# scrimmage plays: runs and passes with a down, no kneel-downs, no two-point tries
SCRIM = REG[REG["play_type"].isin(["run", "pass"]) & REG["down"].notna() & REG["qb_kneel"].ne(1)
            & REG["two_point_attempt"].ne(1)].copy()
SCRIM["conv"] = SCRIM["first_down"].eq(1) | SCRIM["touchdown"].eq(1)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- the sneak, 2022-2025 (FTN is_qb_sneak)
SEAS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
_ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(seasons=SEAS).to_pandas()
FTN_KEYS = ["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"]
S4 = SCRIM[SCRIM["season"].isin(SEAS)].merge(
    _ftn[FTN_KEYS + ["is_qb_sneak", "is_rpo", "n_blitzers", "n_pass_rushers"]],
    left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=FTN_KEYS, how="left")
# FTN has no tush-push flag: is_qb_sneak covers the plain sneak and the pushed version alike
S4["sneak"] = S4["is_qb_sneak"].eq(True) & S4["play_type"].eq("run")
ONE = S4[S4["ydstogo"] == 1]
SNK = ONE[ONE["sneak"]]
Z90 = 1.645


def delta_rows(df):
    """Per season: Eagles rate, rest-of-league rate, the difference and its standard error."""
    out = []
    for s in SEAS:
        d = df[df["season"] == s]
        e, r = d[d["posteam"] == "PHI"]["conv"], d[d["posteam"] != "PHI"]["conv"]
        se = np.sqrt(e.mean() * (1 - e.mean()) / len(e) + r.mean() * (1 - r.mean()) / len(r))
        out.append(dict(season=s, n=len(e), phi=e.mean(), rest=r.mean(), d=e.mean() - r.mean(), se=se))
    return pd.DataFrame(out).set_index("season")


DS = delta_rows(SNK)          # sneaks only
DA = delta_rows(ONE)          # every 1-yard-to-go snap, whatever the call (no play-choice selection)
SN_PHI = SNK[SNK["posteam"] == "PHI"]["conv"]
SN_REST = SNK[SNK["posteam"] != "PHI"]["conv"]
USE = ONE.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["sneak"].mean().unstack()      # share of 1-to-go snaps that were sneaks
USE_PHI = ONE[ONE["posteam"] == "PHI"]["sneak"].mean()
USE_MED = ONE.groupby("posteam")["sneak"].mean().median()
OTHER_RUN = ONE[(ONE["play_type"] == "run") & ~ONE["sneak"] & ONE["qb_scramble"].ne(1)]["conv"].mean()
OTHER_PASS = ONE[ONE["qb_dropback"] == 1]["conv"].mean()
assert DS.loc[2023, "d"] > 0.08 and DS.loc[2025, "d"] < -0.05, "the sneak delta changed shape: re-read the text"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- RPOs (FTN is_rpo), 2022
_rp = S4[S4["is_rpo"].notna() & (S4["season"] == 2022)]
RPO22 = _rp.groupby("posteam")["is_rpo"].mean()
RPO22_LG = _rp["is_rpo"].mean()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- the offense by season, 2021-2025
RUNS = SCRIM[(SCRIM["play_type"] == "run") & SCRIM["qb_scramble"].ne(1)]
DROP = SCRIM[SCRIM["qb_dropback"] == 1]
OC = {2021: "Steichen", 2022: "Steichen", 2023: "B. Johnson", 2024: "Moore", 2025: "Patullo"}
EPA = pd.DataFrame({
    "run": [RUNS[(RUNS["season"] == s) & (RUNS["posteam"] == "PHI")]["epa"].mean()
            - RUNS[RUNS["season"] == s]["epa"].mean() for s in OC],
    "drop": [DROP[(DROP["season"] == s) & (DROP["posteam"] == "PHI")]["epa"].mean()
             - DROP[DROP["season"] == s]["epa"].mean() for s in OC]}, index=list(OC))
OFF_RANK = {s: SCRIM[SCRIM["season"] == s].groupby("posteam")["epa"].mean().rank(ascending=False)["PHI"] for s in OC}
DEF_RANK = {s: SCRIM[SCRIM["season"] == s].groupby("defteam")["epa"].mean().rank()["PHI"] for s in range(2016, 2026)}

_21 = SCRIM[(SCRIM["season"] == 2021) & (SCRIM["posteam"] == "PHI")]
RUN21_EARLY = (_21[_21["week"] <= 7]["play_type"] == "run").mean()
RUN21_LATE = (_21[_21["week"] >= 8]["play_type"] == "run").mean()
_ry = REG.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["rushing_yards"].sum().unstack() / 17
RUSH_YPG = {s: _ry.loc[s, "PHI"] for s in (2021, 2024, 2025)}
RUSH_RANK = {s: _ry.loc[s].rank(ascending=False)["PHI"] for s in (2021, 2024, 2025)}

_24 = SCRIM[SCRIM["season"] == 2024]
RUNSHARE24 = _24.groupby("posteam")["play_type"].apply(lambda x: (x == "run").mean())
BARKLEY_REG = REG[(REG["season"] == 2024) & (REG["rusher_player_name"] == "S.Barkley")]["rushing_yards"].sum()
BARKLEY_POST = ALL[(ALL["season"] == 2024) & (ALL["season_type"] == "POST")
                   & (ALL["rusher_player_name"] == "S.Barkley")]["rushing_yards"].sum()

_f17 = SCRIM[(SCRIM["season"] == 2017) & (SCRIM["down"] == 4)]
GO17 = _f17.groupby("posteam").size()
GO17_CONV = _f17[_f17["posteam"] == "PHI"]["fourth_down_converted"].mean()
_sk = REG[(REG["sack"] == 1) & (REG["season"] == 2022)].groupby("defteam").size()
SACKS22 = int(_sk["PHI"])
assert BARKLEY_REG == 2005 and SACKS22 == 70

_pp = nfl().load_participation(seasons=[2024, 2025]).to_pandas()[["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "defenders_in_box"]]
_bx = SCRIM[SCRIM["season"].isin([2024, 2025]) & SCRIM["down"].isin([1, 2])].merge(
    _pp, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"], how="inner")
_bx["heavy"] = _bx["defenders_in_box"] >= 7
BOX7 = _bx[_bx["posteam"] == "PHI"].groupby("season")["heavy"].mean()
BOX7_RANK = _bx[_bx["season"] == 2025].groupby("posteam")["heavy"].mean().rank(ascending=False, method="min")["PHI"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Super Bowl LIX and the 2024 pass rush
_p24 = nfl().load_participation(seasons=[2024]).to_pandas()[
    ["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "was_pressure", "defense_coverage_type"]]
_ftn24 = nfl().load_ftn_charting(seasons=[2024]).to_pandas()[FTN_KEYS + ["n_blitzers", "n_pass_rushers"]]
_lix = pbp([2024], columns=["game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "qb_dropback", "two_point_attempt", "sack", "season_type",
                            "down", "defteam"])
_lix = (_lix.merge(_ftn24, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=FTN_KEYS, how="left")
        .merge(_p24, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"], how="left",
               suffixes=("", "_p")))
SB = _lix[(_lix["game_id"] == "2024_22_KC_PHI") & (_lix["posteam"] == "KC") & (_lix["qb_dropback"] == 1)]
SB_SCR = SB[SB["two_point_attempt"].ne(1)]
LIX = dict(db=len(SB_SCR), all=len(SB), blitz=int((SB_SCR["n_blitzers"] > 0).sum()),
           four=int((SB["n_pass_rushers"] == 4).sum()), le4=int((SB["n_pass_rushers"] <= 4).sum()),
           c4=int((SB["defense_coverage_type"] == "COVER_4").sum()),
           two=int(SB["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["COVER_2", "2_MAN", "COVER_4", "COVER_6"]).sum()),
           press=int(SB["was_pressure"].eq(True).sum()), sacks=int(SB["sack"].sum()))
_d24 = _lix[(_lix["season_type"] == "REG") & (_lix["qb_dropback"] == 1) & _lix["down"].notna()
            & _lix["n_blitzers"].notna()].copy()
_d24["bl"] = _d24["n_blitzers"] > 0
BLITZ24 = _d24.groupby("defteam")["bl"].mean()
BLITZ24_LG = _d24["bl"].mean()
_cv = _d24[_d24["defense_coverage_type"].notna() & ~_d24["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["BLOWN", "COMBO"])]
TWOHIGH24_PHI = _cv[_cv["defteam"] == "PHI"]["defense_coverage_type"].isin(
    ["COVER_2", "2_MAN", "COVER_4", "COVER_6"]).mean()
assert LIX["blitz"] <= 1 and LIX["sacks"] == 6

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- roster building: draft capital and cap share
_dp = nfl().load_draft_picks().to_pandas()
_dp = _dp[_dp["season"].between(2013, 2025) & (_dp["round"] <= 2)].copy()
_dp["line"] = _dp["position"].isin(["T", "G", "C", "OL", "OT", "OG", "DE", "DT", "DL", "NT"])
DRAFT = _dp.groupby("team")["line"].agg(n="size", k="sum", share="mean")
DRAFT_RANK = DRAFT["share"].rank(ascending=False, method="min")["PHI"]

_c = nfl().load_contracts().to_pandas()
_rows, _seen = [], set()
for _, row in _c.iterrows():          # one row per player-season-team from each contract's season history
    for s in (row["season_history"] if row["season_history"] is not None else []):
        key = (row["otc_id"], s.get("year"), s.get("team"))
        if key in _seen or s.get("year") in (None, ""):
            continue
        _seen.add(key)
        _rows.append(dict(pos=row["position"], year=s.get("year"), team=s.get("team"), cap=s.get("cap_percent")))
CAP = pd.DataFrame(_rows)
CAP["year"] = pd.to_numeric(CAP["year"], errors="coerce")
CAP = CAP[CAP["year"].between(2017, 2025) & CAP["pos"].isin(["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"])]
_ol = CAP.groupby(["year", "team"])["cap"].sum().unstack()
OL_RANKS = _ol.rank(axis=1, ascending=False)["Eagles"]
OL_PHI_MEAN, OL_MED_MEAN = _ol["Eagles"].mean(), _ol.median(axis=1).mean()
```

Third-and-1 at midfield, and everybody in the stadium knows what is coming. The Philadelphia quarterback
crouches under center. Two teammates line up so close behind him that they could rest their hands on his
hips. The defense crowds the middle, linebackers rocking on their toes, ready to leap the pile. The broadcast
cuts to a graphic about how often this works, the snap comes, the whole mass lurches forward, and the chains
move. Seven years earlier the same franchise won its first Super Bowl with the most famous *trick* play of
the century, a play built entirely on the defense not knowing what was coming. How does one team become
famous for both? And is its signature yard really the edge everyone thinks it is? This chapter is about a
franchise that answered the hardest question in roster building ("what do you build around when the
quarterback, the coordinator and the scheme keep changing?") with an unfashionable answer: the two lines of
scrimmage.

**You'll be able to:**

- Explain how the 2017 Eagles used RPOs and an aggressive fourth-down approach to win a Super Bowl with
  their backup quarterback, and diagram the **Philly Special** step by step, saying why the defense
  lost track of the man who caught it.
- Describe the Sirianni-era offense (a run game built on Jalen Hurts's legs and Jeff Stoutland's offensive
  line), recognize its duo and outside-zone runs with Saquon Barkley, and read the coordinator churn in the
  data.
- Measure the tush push as a talent edge: the Eagles' sneak success minus the league's, why that number
  is smaller and noisier than its reputation, and why volume and selection matter more than rate.
- Explain the 2024 champions: Barkley's season, Vic Fangio's defense, and how Super Bowl LIX was won with
  four pass rushers and no blitzes.
- Connect the roster to the scheme: what the Eagles paid for, what they developed, and what a team gets when it
  invests in its lines rather than its skill positions.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd)**: the league since about 2017, when defenses
  answered spread passing by playing two deep safeties and offenses answered back with heavier personnel,
  more runs and more snaps from under center. The Eagles' run game and Fangio's defense are both chapters of
  that story.
- **[Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)**:
  how the [**tush push**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tush-push) works (a quarterback sneak with two
  or three teammates shoving him from behind), the mid-2000s rule change that made it legal, the 2025 ban
  vote, and the league-wide sneak numbers. This chapter builds on all of it and doesn't redraw the play.
- Helpful too: [RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) (a run with a built-in throw, decided by one
  defender after the snap), [Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) and
  [Gap Schemes](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) (outside zone and duo), and the
  [eligibility rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) from
  Formation Rules (who may catch a forward pass).
:::

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and *left* and *right* always
mean the offense's. On offense, Q is the quarterback, R the running back, X and Z wide receivers, H a slot
receiver, Y and U tight ends, and C the center; the other linemen are unlettered. On defense, E and T are the
ends and tackles of the defensive line, M and W linebackers, \$ the nickel back (the fifth defensive back), CB
a cornerback, and SS and FS the safeties. Solid blue arrows are routes, the thick dark arrow is the ball
carrier, lines ending in a short bar are blocks, solid orange arrows are pass rushers, dashed orange lines are
a defender's path, shaded ovals are zones, and brown dashes are the ball in the air. The yellow line is the
line to gain.

## The problem: a franchise built to outlast its quarterbacks

Every NFL team says it builds around its quarterback. The Eagles of the last decade had a harder problem:
their quarterback situation kept changing under them. In 2017 the starter, Carson Wentz, tore his ACL in
December, and the Super Bowl was won by his backup. In 2020 the team drafted Jalen Hurts in the second round,
a pick many questioned barely a year after Wentz had signed a long extension, and within a year he was the starter in an offense rebuilt to suit him.
Around the quarterback, the play-callers changed too: Philadelphia has had five offensive coordinators in
Nick Sirianni's six seasons as head coach.

What did *not* change, for more than a decade, was the line of scrimmage. Look at who stayed:[^constants]

| Constant | Role | Years with the Eagles |
|---|---|---|
| Howie Roseman | General manager (the man who builds the roster) | 2010–2014 and 2016–present (Chip Kelly controlled the roster in 2015) |
| Jeff Stoutland | Offensive line coach | 2013–2025 |
| Lane Johnson | Right tackle (4th overall pick, 2013) | 2013–present (2026 is his 14th season) |
| Jason Kelce | Center (6th-round pick, 2011) | 2011–2023 |

That table is the thesis of this chapter. The Eagles treated their two lines as the part of the team that
lasts, and everything else (the quarterback, the play-caller, the scheme of the season) as the part that
changes. It is not the fashionable approach. Modern team building chases the highest-impact positions:
the quarterback first, then the players who rush the passer and those who catch or cover passes. Offensive linemen
and run-stuffing tackles are often treated as the places to save money. Philadelphia's bet was that an elite
line makes *every* quarterback better, survives every coordinator, and turns ordinary plays (a sneak, an
inside run, a four-man rush) into extraordinary ones.

The rest of the chapter tests that bet across three Super Bowl teams: 2017, 2022 and 2024.

## 2017: RPOs, a backup quarterback, and an aggressive coach

Doug Pederson came to Philadelphia in 2016 from Andy Reid's staff in Kansas City, and he brought Reid's
offense with him, including its fondness for the
[**RPO**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rpo) (run-pass option), a run play with a quick throw attached
that the quarterback chooses between after the snap by watching one defender. By Pro Football Focus's
count, the 2017 Eagles ranked second in the league in RPO usage, behind only Reid's Chiefs.[^pfftree]
[RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) tells the mechanics and that season's story in full; here is
what matters for this case study.

**The RPO as a quarterback simplifier.** Wentz was playing at an MVP level when he tore his ACL against the
Rams on December 10, 2017. His backup, Nick Foles, was a pocket passer with a fine arm and none of Wentz's
improvising. The coaches leaned harder on RPOs, because an RPO hands the quarterback his answer: if the
defender he is reading plays the run, throw; if he drops into coverage, hand off. A quarterback who reads one
man and throws on time does not need to be a star. By PFF's charting, Foles completed 15 of his 16 RPO throws in
his first five starts after the injury,[^foles] and in the playoffs the Eagles scored 38 points against the league's best defense in the NFC Championship
and 41 in the Super Bowl.

**An offensive line that made the run real.** An RPO only works if the run part is a real threat. If the
defense can stop the handoff with the players it already has in the box, it never has to choose. The 2017 line
(Jason Peters at left tackle until he tore his ACL and MCL on October 23, then Halapoulivaati Vaitai;[^peters] Stefen Wisniewski, Kelce,
Brandon Brooks and Lane Johnson inside and at right tackle) was one of the best in football, and Jay Ajayi, LeGarrette Blount and
Corey Clement ran behind it.

**Aggression on fourth down.** Pederson was also one of the first NFL coaches to act on what analysts had
been saying for years: that teams punt and kick far too often on fourth-and-short. An analyst on his staff,
Ryan Paganetti, sat on the headset during games feeding him the math on fourth downs.[^paganetti] In 2017 the Eagles went
for it on fourth down `{python} int(GO17["PHI"])` times, the `{python} nth(GO17.rank(ascending=False, method="min")["PHI"])`-most
in the league, and converted `{python} pct(GO17_CONV)`.[^go17] That habit produced the two most important
snaps of their Super Bowl. One was fourth-and-1 at their own 45 with 5:39 left, trailing New England 33–32:
Foles threw to Zach Ertz for two yards, and the drive ended with Ertz's go-ahead touchdown. The other was the
most famous trick play of the century.

### The Philly Special

Super Bowl LII, February 4, 2018, in Minneapolis. The Eagles led New England 15–12 with 38 seconds left in
the first half and faced fourth-and-goal from the 1. Almost every coach of that era would have kicked the
field goal. During a timeout, Foles walked over to Pederson and asked, in words a sideline microphone
caught, "You want Philly Philly?" Pederson paused, then said, "Yeah, let's do it."[^ps]

The play they called is the [**Philly Special**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-philly-special): the
quarterback walks up to the line as if changing the play, the ball is snapped directly to the running back,
who pitches it to a tight end running the other way, and the tight end throws to the quarterback, who has
drifted into the end zone unnoticed. @fig-philly-special shows it from the snap to the catch.

```{python}
#| label: fig-philly-special
#| fig-cap: "The Philly Special, Super Bowl LII, fourth-and-goal from the 1 (simulated, BDB-format tracking generated by gridiron, not recorded; alignments follow film breakdowns of the play, with defenders' exact spots approximate). Foles (Q, ringed) starts in the shotgun with Corey Clement (R), who has motioned in, behind him; Torrey Smith (Z) and Trey Burton (Y) are stacked on the left with Zach Ertz (U) beside them, and Alshon Jeffery (X) is alone on the right. 1: Foles walks up behind the right tackle, gesturing as if to change the play. 2: the ball is snapped straight to Clement, who runs left; the linebacker over the middle (M) and the defenders on the left chase him. 3: Clement pitches to Burton, coming back the other way on a reverse. 4: Burton, a high-school quarterback, throws to Foles, who has walked into the right side of the end zone with nobody within three yards of him."
def philly_special():
    """Every body keyframed by hand: (t, d, w) waypoints, t in seconds from the snap."""
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -4.2, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.0, 0.0, "R"),
                     O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, -7.4, "Z"), O("Y", "TE", -2.6, -7.4, "Y"),
                     O("U", "TE", -1.6, -5.4, "U"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, 12.0, "X")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 0.8, -4.4, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 0.8, -0.9, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 0.8, 0.9, "T"),
           D("RE", "DE", 0.8, 4.4, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 2.3, -1.4, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 2.2, 3.3, "W"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 1.8, -9.0, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 2.8, -6.4, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 4.2, -3.4, "SS"),
           D("RCB", "CB", 1.6, 12.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 6.4, 1.2, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(1), to_go=1)
    T = {
        # Foles walks up behind the right tackle and stands there through the snap, then drifts right
        "QB": [(-2.0, -4.2, 0.0), (-0.7, -1.9, 3.9), (0.7, -1.9, 3.9), (1.2, -1.0, 5.3), (1.9, 1.4, 5.7),
               (2.5, 2.7, 5.9)],
        # Clement: direct snap, runs left, pitches at +1.0, carries out the fake
        "RB": [(0.0, -6.0, 0.0), (0.35, -5.9, -0.5), (0.7, -6.2, -2.0), (1.0, -6.4, -3.4), (1.6, -6.0, -6.4),
               (2.2, -5.6, -7.6)],
        # Burton: from behind Smith, back across the formation; takes the pitch, rolls right, throws at +2.0
        "Y": [(0.0, -2.6, -7.4), (0.5, -3.6, -6.2), (1.0, -4.6, -3.6), (1.3, -5.0, -1.0), (1.7, -5.4, 1.6),
              (2.0, -5.2, 3.4), (2.6, -4.9, 4.2)],
        # Smith: across the end zone as the second option; Ertz seals the left end; Jeffery takes his corner deep
        "Z": [(0.0, LINE_D, -7.4), (0.6, 1.6, -6.6), (1.3, 4.4, -3.0), (2.0, 5.6, 0.0), (2.6, 5.9, 1.4)],
        "U": [(0.0, -1.6, -5.4), (0.5, -0.5, -5.3)],
        "X": [(0.0, LINE_D, 12.0), (0.8, 3.4, 11.6), (1.6, 7.4, 9.8), (2.6, 8.6, 8.4)],
        "LT": [(0.0, LINE_D, -3.2), (0.4, -0.5, -3.2)], "LG": [(0.0, LINE_D, -1.6), (0.4, -0.5, -1.6)],
        "C": [(0.0, LINE_D, 0.0), (0.4, -0.5, 0.0)], "RG": [(0.0, LINE_D, 1.6), (0.4, -0.5, 1.6)],
        "RT": [(0.0, LINE_D, 3.2), (0.4, -0.5, 3.2)],
        # the defense: everyone near the ball flows left with the run; the backside players lose Foles
        "LE": [(0.0, 0.8, -4.4), (0.5, 0.9, -4.9)],
        "LT_": [(0.0, 0.8, -0.9), (0.4, 0.75, -0.9)], "RT_": [(0.0, 0.8, 0.9), (0.4, 0.75, 0.9)],
        "RE": [(0.0, 0.8, 4.4), (0.6, 0.3, 5.2), (1.1, -2.0, 7.0), (2.0, -3.4, 6.2), (2.6, -3.6, 5.4)],
        "MIKE": [(0.0, 2.3, -1.4), (0.8, 2.0, -3.4), (1.3, 1.9, -3.6), (2.0, 1.8, -2.0), (2.6, 2.2, -0.2)],
        "WILL": [(0.0, 2.2, 3.3), (0.7, 1.9, 1.8), (1.4, 2.1, 1.0), (2.0, 2.0, 2.0), (2.6, 2.0, 3.1)],
        "LCB": [(0.0, 1.8, -9.0), (0.6, 3.4, -8.4), (1.3, 3.0, -4.4), (2.0, 4.2, -1.4), (2.6, 4.6, -0.2)],
        "NB": [(0.0, 2.8, -6.4), (0.7, 1.2, -8.4), (1.2, 0.4, -8.2), (1.9, 1.4, -6.6), (2.6, 2.3, -5.2)],
        "SS": [(0.0, 4.2, -3.4), (0.7, 4.6, -5.2), (1.3, 4.6, -5.6), (1.9, 3.8, -3.6), (2.6, 3.4, -2.0)],
        "RCB": [(0.0, 1.6, 12.0), (0.8, 3.6, 13.2), (1.6, 7.4, 11.4), (2.6, 8.8, 10.0)],
        "FS": [(0.0, 6.4, 1.2), (0.8, 6.2, 0.0), (1.6, 6.2, 1.0), (2.6, 5.8, 3.0)],
    }
    set_tracks(p, {k: ease([(-2.6, p.players[k].d, p.players[k].w)] + v) for k, v in T.items()})
    return p


def ps_ball_at(p, t):
    """Where the ball is: on the ground at the snap, then to Clement, Burton and Foles in turn."""
    if t <= 0.0:
        return np.array([0.0, 0.0]), False
    if t < 0.35:
        return (p.position("RB", 0.35) + [0.95, 0.0]) * t / 0.35, False
    if t < 1.0:
        return p.position("RB", t) + [0.95, 0.0], False
    if t < 1.15:
        a, b = p.position("RB", 1.0) + [0.95, 0.0], p.position("Y", 1.15) + [0.95, 0.0]
        return a + (b - a) * (t - 1.0) / 0.15, False
    if t < 2.0:
        return p.position("Y", t) + [0.95, 0.0], False
    if t < 2.55:
        a, b = p.position("Y", 2.0) + [0.95, 0.0], p.position("QB", 2.55) + [0.95, 0.0]
        return a + (b - a) * (t - 2.0) / 0.55, True
    return p.position("QB", t) + [0.95, 0.0], False


def ps_deco(t, fld, p):
    """The ball, Foles's walk before the snap (dashed) and the throw (brown dashes)."""
    walk = np.array([p.position("QB", tt) for tt in np.linspace(-2.0, min(t, -0.7), 20)]) if t > -2.0 else None
    if walk is not None:
        xs, ys = P(fld, p, walk[:, 0], walk[:, 1])
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=4)
    if t > 2.0:
        a = p.position("Y", 2.0) + [0.95, 0.0]
        ts = np.linspace(2.0, min(t, 2.55), 12)
        b = np.array([ps_ball_at(p, tt)[0] for tt in ts])
        xs, ys = P(fld, p, np.r_[a[0], b[:, 0]], np.r_[a[1], b[:, 1]])
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9)
    if t <= 0.0:
        return                       # before the snap the ball is under the center's hand
    bd, bw = ps_ball_at(p, t)[0]
    x, y = P(fld, p, bd, bw)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), 0.95, 0.6, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=12))


PS = philly_special()
PS_T = [-1.1, 0.6, 1.1, 2.6]
PS_N = ["Foles walks up behind the right\ntackle as if changing the play.",
        "Direct snap to Clement, who runs\nleft. The defense flows with him.",
        "Clement pitches to Burton,\ncoming back the other way.",
        "Burton throws to Foles, alone in\nthe end zone. Touchdown."]
PS_LAT, PS_WIN = (-12.5, 15.5), (-8.5, 12.0)
if PDF:
    strip_grid(PS, PS_T, PS_N, PS_LAT, PS_WIN, rings=(("QB", style.THIRD),), deco=ps_deco, ltg=False, mr=0.62)
    plt.show()
else:
    video(PS, PS_LAT, PS_WIN, 2.9, rings=(("QB", style.THIRD),), notes=PS_N, times=PS_T, t_start=-2.2,
          deco=ps_deco, ltg=False, mr=0.62)
```

Take it a step at a time, because each step has a reason.

1. **Foles walks up and becomes a receiver.** A quarterback lined up directly behind the center, taking the
   snap from his hands, is not an eligible receiver; a quarterback in the shotgun is just a back, and
   backs can catch passes. When Foles walked forward and stood behind his right tackle, at least a yard off
   the line, he was a back like any other. The gesturing, the shouted words and the walk itself all told the
   defense he was changing the protection, the most ordinary thing a quarterback does before a snap. At the
   snap he did nothing for a beat, which is the hardest part of selling it.
2. **The direct snap goes to the running back.** Kelce snapped the ball straight to Clement. To eleven
   defenders, a running back with the ball on the 1-yard line means *a run*, and every one of them has a
   run responsibility. The linebackers and the defenders on Clement's side chased him.
3. **The reverse brings the ball back.** Clement pitched to Burton, a tight end coming the other way. A
   reverse is a misdirection play by itself; here it moved the ball away from the defenders who had just
   committed to Clement.
4. **The throw.** Burton had played quarterback in high school and taken snaps at quarterback at Florida. He rolled
   right and lobbed the ball to Foles, who had walked into the end zone after every defender near him had turned toward
   the run and nobody had stayed with him. Torrey Smith, crossing the end
   zone, was a second option Burton didn't need.

Why does it work? Because the defense's rules, not its effort, let it down. At the goal line every defender
has a gap to fill or a receiver to cover, and nobody has "the quarterback," because the quarterback is the
one player a defense never has to cover. The play turns that rule into a hole. It also lands at the perfect
moment: fourth-and-goal from the 1 is when a defense is most committed to stopping the run, and least
able to think about anything else.

What it gives up is just as clear. A trick play is a one-time bet. If a single defender stays home on the
quarterback, Burton is rolling right with the ball and nowhere to throw it, on fourth down. And it can only
fool a defense that hasn't seen it, so its value falls every time it's run.

It wasn't new, either. The Eagles found it on film of the Chicago Bears, who had run a version of it for a
touchdown against Minnesota late in the 2016 season and called it the "Clemson Special," after a college
team that had used it years before. Wide receivers coach Mike Groh, who had coached in Chicago, helped
install it, and the Eagles had considered running it in the NFC Championship Game before the score made it
unnecessary.[^origin] Even the alignment was argued about afterward: the former officiating chief Mike
Pereira said Alshon Jeffery, alone on the right, was a step off the line, which would have left only six
players on it and made it an illegal formation. Jeffery had checked with the official before the snap, and
no flag was thrown.[^formation]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The Philly Special was a gamble a coach dreamed up on the sideline." It was a gamble, but not an improvised
one. The play had been installed and practised for the playoffs, the coaches had chosen the situation for it
in advance, and the quarterback asked for it by name. What *was* bold was the decision to go for it on
fourth down at all, and that was the 2017 Eagles' habit, not a one-off. Trick plays look like inspiration;
they are usually homework.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2017"}
**The season:** 13–3 and the NFC's top seed, despite losing Wentz, Peters and other starters to injury; a
38–7 win over Minnesota in the NFC Championship, then a 41–33 win over New England in Super Bowl LII, with
Foles the game's MVP.[^lii]

**What to notice on the Super Bowl film:** the Philly Special is the famous snap, but watch the fourth-and-1
at the Eagles' 45 with 5:39 left in the fourth quarter. The Eagles were behind by a point. A punt would have
given Tom Brady the ball with a lead and five minutes to run out the clock. Instead Foles took a shotgun snap
and threw a quick pass to Ertz in the flat for two yards. The drive ended with Ertz's touchdown catch that put
Philadelphia ahead for good. The same coach made both fourth-down calls in the same game, and the same
reasoning was behind each: a yard is usually worth more than the kick.
:::

## 2021–2025: Sirianni, Hurts, and a run game built in the trenches

Pederson was fired after the 2020 season, and Nick Sirianni, the Colts' offensive coordinator, replaced him
in January 2021. His first offense started like most modern offenses: in the shotgun, throwing the ball. After
seven games the Eagles were 2–5, and two things changed at once. Sirianni handed play-calling to his
offensive coordinator, Shane Steichen, and the offense turned around. In weeks 1–7 the Eagles ran on
`{python} pct(RUN21_EARLY)` of their snaps; from week 8 on, on `{python} pct(RUN21_LATE)`. They won seven of
their last ten games, made the playoffs, and led the league in rushing at
`{python} f"{RUSH_YPG[2021]:.0f}"` yards a game.[^pivot]

Why would a modern offense get *better* by running more? Because of who was running it.

### The quarterback as an extra blocker

On a normal handoff, the quarterback gives the ball away and stops mattering, so the offense blocks with
ten players against eleven defenders. Jalen Hurts is strong, fast and hard to tackle, so a defense has to
account for him on every snap, and that changes the arithmetic. On a
[zone read](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) one defender is left unblocked, and Hurts reads him:
hand off if that defender crashes inside, keep it if he stays outside. On a designed quarterback run (QB power
or QB counter), the running back becomes a blocker. Either way the offense blocks with one more player than
usual, the "extra hat" of [Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd).

The RPO came back too, now with a quarterback who could also run. In 2022, FTN's charting has Philadelphia
using RPOs on `{python} pct(RPO22["PHI"])` of its plays, more than any other team and well above the league's
`{python} pct(RPO22_LG)`.[^rpo22] A single snap could hand off, keep or throw, and the defender being read had
to be wrong about at least one of them.

### The line, and the man who coached it

None of that works without the five men in front. Jeff Stoutland came to Philadelphia in 2013 from Nick
Saban's Alabama, hired by Chip Kelly, and he stayed through Pederson and Sirianni. That run is rare in a
league where position coaches usually leave with the head coach who hired them. He was the Eagles' run game
coordinator as well as their line coach, and his reputation rested on turning unlikely players into
starters:

- **Jordan Mailata**, an Australian rugby league player who had never played a down of American football,
  was a seventh-round pick in 2018. He made his first starts in 2020, was the full-time left tackle from 2021,
  and in 2024 signed a three-year, $66 million extension that made him one of the four highest-paid tackles in
  the league.
- **Jason Kelce**, a sixth-round pick in 2011 and small for a center, became a six-time first-team All-Pro.
  His speed off the ball suited the Eagles' zone and screen game, and his timing made their sneak the most feared
  in football.
- **Mekhi Becton**, a former first-round pick the Jets had given up on as a tackle, signed a one-year deal in
  2024, moved inside to right guard at the Eagles' request, and started 15 games for a Super Bowl champion.[^becton]

@fig-barkley-runs shows the two runs that line was built for in 2024, with Saquon Barkley carrying.

```{python}
#| label: fig-barkley-runs
#| fig-cap: "The two runs at the heart of the 2024 Eagles' ground game, drawn against a two-high nickel defense (illustrative, not one specific play; the wide receivers are off the picture). Left, duo from the shotgun: two double teams (green ovals) drive the defensive tackles straight back; whichever linebacker fills, a lineman comes off the double to meet him (green dashes), and Barkley (R, ringed) presses the doubles and reads the Mike, hitting the gap he doesn't fill. Right, outside zone from the pistol: every blocker steps toward the right sideline together, the tight end reaches the end, and Barkley aims at the tight end's outside leg, then cuts up or back wherever a seam opens. Six blockers against six in the box, with two safeties twelve yards deep: the light box that a two-high defense concedes."
def nickel_two_high():
    """Even front, two linebackers, the nickel over the slot, two safeties deep: six in the box."""
    return [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.3, "T"),
            D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.9, "E"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.6, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.6, 1.4, "M"),
            D("NB", "NB", 4.2, -8.0, "$"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -6.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 6.5, "SS")]


def eagles_11(qb_d, rb):
    return line5() + [O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8, "Y"), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -8.6, "H"),
                      O("QB", "QB", qb_d, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", *rb, "R")]


def pair_oval(fld, p, d, w, wid=3.0, dep=2.6):
    x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), wid, dep, fc=style.THIRD, alpha=0.22, ec=style.THIRD, lw=0.9,
                             zorder=1.7))


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
LAT, WIN = (-10.6, 10.6), (-9.8, 14.2)

# --- duo from the gun
p = Play(eagles_11(GUN, (GUN, -2.1)), nickel_two_high(), los=own(35), to_go=None)
for k, end in (("LG", (0.25, -1.15)), ("C", (0.25, -0.45)), ("RG", (0.25, 1.95)), ("RT", (0.25, 2.65)),
               ("Y", (0.35, 5.4)), ("LT", (0.35, -3.6))):
    move_to(p, k, end)
move_to(p, "RB", (-2.4, 0.8), (0.3, 0.8), kind="run")
p.highlight("RB")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
pair_oval(f, p, 0.4, -0.8)
pair_oval(f, p, 0.4, 2.3)
branch(f, p, [(1.6, -1.0), (3.9, -2.0)], color=READ_GREEN, end="bar", lw=1.3)
branch(f, p, [(1.6, 2.2), (3.9, 1.6)], color=READ_GREEN, end="bar", lw=1.3)
branch(f, p, [(0.3, 0.8), (3.0, 0.7)], color=OD, lw=1.3)
branch(f, p, [(0.3, 0.8), (3.2, 3.4)], color=OD, lw=1.3)
say(f, p, 8.5, 0.0, "6 in the box vs 6 blockers", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -7.6, 5.0, "doubles drive the\ntackles back", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=6.4)
point_to(f, p, (-7.6, -5.4), (-5.0, -2.1), "R reads the Mike:\nA gap or B gap", color=OD, fontsize=6.4)
panel_title(axes[0], "Duo: straight ahead")

# --- outside zone from the pistol
p = Play(eagles_11(PISTOL, (-7.0, 0.0)), nickel_two_high(), los=own(35), to_go=None)
for k, end in (("LT", (0.2, -1.9)), ("LG", (2.4, -1.6)), ("C", (0.3, 0.2)), ("RG", (0.3, 2.9)),
               ("RT", (0.4, 4.6)), ("Y", (0.4, 6.6))):
    move_to(p, k, end)
move_to(p, "RB", (-4.0, 3.0), (-1.5, 6.3), kind="run")
p.highlight("RB")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
branch(f, p, [(-1.5, 6.3), (2.6, 9.0)], color=OD, lw=1.3)
branch(f, p, [(-1.5, 6.3), (3.2, 3.4)], color=OD, lw=1.3)
say(f, p, 8.5, 0.0, "the whole line steps right", color=OD, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (-7.6, 5.6), (-2.6, 5.1), "aim at Y's outside\nleg, then cut", color=OD, fontsize=6.4)
say(f, p, -7.6, -5.4, "backside linemen\ncut off pursuit", color=OD, fontsize=6.4)
panel_title(axes[1], "Outside zone: across, then up")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
field_legend(axes[0], ["carrier", "block", "double", "climb"], y=-0.01, ncol=4)
axes[0].get_legend().set_bbox_to_anchor((1.05, -0.01))
plt.show()
```

The two plays ask different things of the line, and the Eagles' line could do both. **Duo** (from
[Gap Schemes](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)) is a straight-ahead shoving match: two double
teams move the two defensive tackles backward, and the back runs through whichever gap the Mike linebacker
leaves open. It needs linemen strong enough to move a 300-pound man two yards against his will.
[**Outside zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-outside-zone) (from
[Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)) is a race: the whole line steps sideways together,
the defense has to run with it, and somewhere a defender overruns his gap and opens a seam for the back to cut
through. It needs linemen quick enough to get their heads across a defender's body. Johnson, Mailata, Landon
Dickerson and Kelce (and from 2024 his successor at center, Cam Jurgens) were rare in being good at both.

Why did that matter so much in 2024? Because of what defenses were doing. Across the league, defenses were
playing more and more [**two-high**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) coverage, keeping both safeties
deep to stop explosive passes, which leaves only six defenders near the line: a
[**light box**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-light-box) ([The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd)
tells that story). A light box is the defense making a bet: we'll give you four or five yards on the ground
rather than twenty in the air. The Eagles' line, with Barkley behind it, made that a losing bet.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Saquon Barkley, 2024"}
**The season:** Barkley signed a three-year contract with the Eagles in March 2024 after six seasons with the
Giants, and ran for `{python} f"{BARKLEY_REG:,.0f}"` yards in the regular season, becoming the ninth player in
NFL history to reach 2,000. Counting his `{python} f"{BARKLEY_POST:,.0f}"` in the playoffs, he ran for
`{python} f"{BARKLEY_REG + BARKLEY_POST:,.0f}"` yards in one season, more than any player before him. He was
the league's Offensive Player of the Year. The Eagles ran the ball on `{python} pct(RUNSHARE24["PHI"])` of their
snaps, the highest share in the league, and averaged `{python} f"{RUSH_YPG[2024]:.0f}"` rushing yards a
game.[^barkley]

**What to notice:** what happens *after* the line has done its job. Barkley is a big back with sprinter's
speed, and in 2024 his long runs came on ordinary-looking plays: duo or zone, a crease at the line, one
missed tackle at the second level, and then nobody left, because two-high safeties start twelve yards deep
and have to come down to make the tackle. A light box gives a back like that one chance at the safeties.
Count, on his long runs, how many defenders are within three yards of the line of scrimmage at the snap.
:::

### The coordinator churn

If the line was the constant, the play-caller was the variable. Look at the list:

| Season | Offensive coordinator | What happened next |
|---|---|---|
| 2021–2022 | Shane Steichen (play-caller from midway through 2021) | Hired as the Colts' head coach, February 2023 |
| 2023 | Brian Johnson | Not retained after a late-season collapse |
| 2024 | Kellen Moore | Hired as the Saints' head coach, February 2025 |
| 2025 | Kevin Patullo | Replaced after one season |
| 2026 | Sean Mannion (from the Packers, where he coached quarterbacks) | A first-time play-caller, calling the plays in 2026[^mannion26] |

Mannion's hiring in January 2026 made him, in the Associated Press's count, the Eagles' fifth offensive
coordinator in five seasons.[^mannion] Some of the churn is the price of success: Steichen and Moore left
for head-coaching jobs because their offenses had been good. Some of it is not. @fig-oc-churn puts each
season's offense next to its coordinator.

```{python}
#| label: fig-oc-churn
#| fig-cap: "The Eagles' offense against the league, by season and offensive coordinator, 2021–2025 regular seasons: expected points added (EPA) per play on designed runs and on dropbacks, minus the league average (above zero is better than average). The run game stayed well above average under three different coordinators, and the passing game rose with it, until both fell back toward average in 2025. Data: nflverse play-by-play (runs exclude quarterback scrambles, which count as dropbacks)."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.3))
xs = np.arange(len(EPA))
ax.axhline(0, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9)
ax.plot(xs, EPA["run"], marker="o", ms=6, color=style.SERIES[0], label="designed runs")
ax.plot(xs, EPA["drop"], marker="s", ms=5.5, color=style.SERIES[1], label="dropbacks (passes, sacks, scrambles)")
for x, (r, d) in zip(xs, EPA[["run", "drop"]].values):
    ax.text(x, max(r, d) + 0.013, f"{r:+.2f}", ha="center", fontsize=6.8, color=style.SERIES[0])
ax.set_xticks(xs)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"{s}\n{OC[s]}" for s in EPA.index], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per play, Eagles minus league", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 0.17)
ax.set_xlim(-0.4, len(xs) - 0.6)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.legend(fontsize=7.2, loc="lower left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The chart says two things. First, the Eagles' run game was one of the league's best for four straight
seasons under three play-callers, which is what you would expect if the line, more than the coordinator,
was the source of it. ([**EPA**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa), expected points added, scores each play
by how much it changed the offense's expected points; a run game +0.10 above average adds about a point
every ten carries.) Second, in 2025 that edge was gone: the run game finished
`{python} f"{EPA.loc[2025, 'run']:+.2f}"` against the league, roughly average, and the Eagles ran for
`{python} f"{RUSH_YPG[2025]:.0f}"` yards a game, `{python} nth(RUSH_RANK[2025])` in the league. The offense ranked
`{python} nth(OFF_RANK[2025])` in EPA per play.

Be careful with the "why." Several things changed at once in 2025: a new play-caller, a Barkley coming off
the heaviest workload of his career, defenses that crowded the box more often (next section), and, according to
reporting by the *Philadelphia Inquirer* and ESPN, a push by Sirianni and Patullo to diversify the run game
that cut into Stoutland's role as its designer; he lost the title of run game coordinator during the season.
On February 4, 2026, Stoutland announced that he was leaving, after 13 seasons.[^stout] A single season can't
separate those causes. What it can tell you is that the one stable thing in the Eagles' offense was also
the one that slipped.

## The tush push as a talent edge

[Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)
explains how the tush push works and shows that league-wide, quarterback sneaks of every kind (FTN's
`is_qb_sneak` flag covers the plain sneak and the push together) convert about four times in five on 1
yard to go. It ends on a puzzle: the Eagles' conversion rate on the play sits close to the league line,
even though they ran it far more often than anyone, against defenses that knew it was coming. This
section takes that puzzle up. If the push is the Eagles' signature, how big was their edge, really?

The ingredients are not in doubt. Hurts has unusual leg strength for a quarterback. Kelce was famously quick
and low off the ball. Johnson, Mailata and Dickerson were among the best linemen at their positions.
And Stoutland drilled the play's timing until the line moved as one at the instant of the snap. The
question is what those ingredients produced.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sneak-delta
#| fig-cap: "The tush push as an edge: Eagles minus the rest of the league, in percentage points of conversions (first down or touchdown) on 1 yard to go, 2022–2025 regular seasons, with 90% intervals. Blue: quarterback sneaks only (the push and the plain sneak; FTN's is_qb_sneak). Orange: every snap on 1 yard to go, whatever the call, which removes the question of which plays a team chose to sneak on. Only 2023 stands clearly above zero on either measure; by 2025 the Eagles' sneaks converted less often than the league's. The labels under each season give the Eagles' number of sneaks. Data: nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
xs = np.arange(len(SEAS))
ax.axhline(0, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9)
for off, df, c, m, lab in ((-0.12, DS, style.SERIES[0], "o", "sneaks only"),
                           (0.12, DA, style.SERIES[1], "s", "every 1-yard-to-go snap")):
    ax.errorbar(xs + off, 100 * df["d"], yerr=100 * Z90 * df["se"], fmt=m, ms=6, color=c, ecolor=c,
                elinewidth=1.4, capsize=0, alpha=0.95, label=lab)
    for x, v in zip(xs + off, df["d"]):
        ax.text(x + (0.09 if off > 0 else -0.09), 100 * v, f"{100 * v:+.0f}", fontsize=6.8, color=c,
                ha="left" if off > 0 else "right", va="center")
ax.set_xticks(xs)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"{s}\n{int(DS.loc[s, 'n'])} sneaks" for s in SEAS], fontsize=7.5)
ax.axvline(1.5, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 3)))
ax.text(1.52, 27, "Kelce retires\nafter 2023", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
ax.set_ylabel("Eagles minus league,\npercentage points", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(-34, 30)
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(xs) - 0.5)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.legend(fontsize=7.2, loc="lower left", ncol=2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read the blue dots first. Over the four seasons, the Eagles converted `{python} pct(SN_PHI.mean())` of
their `{python} len(SN_PHI)` sneaks on 1 yard to go, and the rest of the league converted
`{python} pct(SN_REST.mean())` of theirs: a difference of about `{python} f"{100 * (SN_PHI.mean() - SN_REST.mean()):.0f}"`
points.[^delta] Season by season, the edge was
`{python} pts_(DS.loc[2022, "d"])` in 2022, `{python} pts_(DS.loc[2023, "d"])` in 2023,
`{python} pts_(DS.loc[2024, "d"])` in 2024 and `{python} pts_(DS.loc[2025, "d"])` in 2025. That is not
what a near-unstoppable play looks like. Three things explain the gap between the reputation and the
numbers, and they are worth learning, because they apply to almost every "Team X is great at Y" claim you
will hear on a broadcast.

**1. Small samples.** Thirty or forty sneaks a season is not many. A play that truly succeeds 82% of the time
will, in a season of 35 tries, land anywhere from about 71% to 93% just by chance. That is what the vertical
bars show, and in three of the four seasons the bar crosses zero. A single good or bad season of sneaks tells
you very little. Four seasons pooled tell you more, and they say: about league average.

**2. Selection.** Every other team chose its sneaks. They ran the play when the ball was spotted inches from
the line to gain, against a defense that looked soft in the middle, and called something else when it
wasn't. The Eagles ran it on `{python} pct(USE_PHI)` of all their 1-yard-to-go snaps in these four seasons,
against a league median of `{python} pct(USE_MED)`: on full yards as well as inches, against defenses that
had a week to plan for it and lined up specifically to stop it. Matching the league's rate while taking the
harder snaps is itself a sign of an edge. That is why the orange dots matter: they compare *every* snap on 1
yard to go, whatever the call, so no team gets to pick its spots. On that measure the Eagles converted more
often than the league in every season, but only 2023, at `{python} pts_(DA.loc[2023, "d"])`, is clearly
more than noise.

**3. Volume is the edge.** Here is the arithmetic that made the push valuable even at a league-average rate.
Across the league, sneaks on 1 yard to go converted `{python} pct(SNK["conv"].mean())`; other runs converted
`{python} pct(OTHER_RUN)` and passes `{python} pct(OTHER_PASS)`. A team that can run its best short-yardage play on
*every* short-yardage snap, without the defense's knowing it was coming dragging the rate down, collects that
difference over and over. Most teams can't: their quarterback isn't built for it, their line can't win the
snap every time, or their coach won't put the starter at the bottom of a pile forty times a year. The Eagles'
talent edge wasn't a higher success rate. It was being able to call the play every time and still convert at
the league's rate.

**And then it faded.** The 2023 season, Kelce's last, was the peak. In 2024 the rate fell back to the league's;
in 2025 the Eagles converted `{python} pct(DS.loc[2025, "phi"])` of their sneaks, well below the rest of the
league's `{python} pct(DS.loc[2025, "rest"])`, and ran fewer of them
(`{python} int(DS.loc[2025, "n"])`). The candidate explanations are the ones in the next section: the center
who timed the snap had retired, defenses had studied the play for three years, and the league told its
officials to watch for linemen moving early. The sample is too small to rank those causes. The direction is not
in doubt.

## 2024: Barkley, Fangio, and a four-man rush

The 2023 Eagles started 10–1 and collapsed, losing six of their last seven games, including a lopsided
wild-card loss in Tampa. The defense was the main culprit: by EPA per play it ranked
`{python} nth(DEF_RANK[2023])` in the league.[^def23] The offseason that followed was the most consequential
in the franchise's recent history:

- **Vic Fangio** was hired as defensive coordinator. Then 65, he had first coached in the NFL in 1986 and
  spent most of the four decades since in the league, and he was the man behind the two-high, light-box
  defenses that had spread across the league from his late-2010s Bears and Broncos[^fangio] (his ideas are the subject of
  [their own case study](12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)). He was still the Eagles' coordinator in 2026.
- **Saquon Barkley** signed as a free agent, the rare case of the Eagles paying a running back.
- The draft brought two rookie defensive backs, cornerback Quinyon Mitchell in the first round and Cooper
  DeJean in the second, who both started on a Super Bowl defense as rookies; Zack Baun, signed to a one-year
  deal as a backup linebacker, became a first-team All-Pro.
- **Kellen Moore** became offensive coordinator, the third in three seasons.

The result was a 14–3 season and a defense that allowed the fewest yards in the league and ranked
`{python} nth(DEF_RANK[2024])` in EPA per play, a year after ranking `{python} nth(DEF_RANK[2023])`.
Fangio's defense blitzed less than most: by FTN's charting, it sent a
[**blitz**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-blitz) (any rusher beyond the defensive linemen) on
`{python} pct(BLITZ24["PHI"])` of dropbacks, `{python} nth(BLITZ24.rank(ascending=False, method="min")["PHI"])`
of 32 teams, against a league rate of `{python} pct(BLITZ24_LG)`.[^blitz24] It trusted four rushers to get
there and kept seven players in coverage. Then, in the Super Bowl, it did that on almost every snap.

### Super Bowl LIX: four rushers, no blitzes

February 9, 2025, New Orleans: Eagles 40, Chiefs 22. The Eagles led 24–0 at halftime and 34–0 late in the third
quarter, and the defense did it without blitzing. NFL Next Gen Stats counted 42 Patrick Mahomes dropbacks and
**zero blitzes**, only the fourth time a defense had gone a whole game without blitzing since it began tracking
in 2014, and still credited the Eagles with 16 pressures, a pressure on 38.1% of dropbacks, and six sacks, the
most Mahomes had taken in a game in his career.[^lix] FTN's charters, counting slightly differently, saw
a blitz on `{python} LIX["blitz"]` of Mahomes's `{python} LIX["db"]` scrimmage dropbacks, and that one came in the
fourth quarter with the game long decided; they had exactly four rushers on `{python} LIX["four"]` of the
`{python} LIX["all"]` dropbacks including two-point tries, and four or fewer on `{python} LIX["le4"]`.[^lixftn]
After the game the defensive end Josh Sweat, who had 2.5 sacks, put it plainly: "Vic didn't want to blitz. We
knew if we had to blitz, we'd be in trouble." @fig-lix-four shows the shape of it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lix-four
#| fig-cap: "The Super Bowl LIX plan, typical snap (illustrative; based on FTN's charting of the game, not one specific play): Kansas City in 11 personnel from the shotgun against the Eagles' nickel. Four rushers (solid orange) take on five linemen and a back who stays in to block; seven defenders drop into coverage, here a quarters shell: four deep defenders each guarding a quarter of the field (CB, FS, SS, CB) and three underneath. Every route has a defender above or beside it, the quarterback has nowhere quick to throw, and the four rushers have time to win one-on-one."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, 2.1, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -19.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -11.0, "H"),
                 O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 8.5, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 18.0, "Z")]
dfn = dline(w=(-5.0, -0.8, 2.4, 5.2)) + [
    D("WILL", "LB", 5.0, -3.0, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 5.0, 2.6, "M"), D("NB", "NB", 4.6, -10.0, "$"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -18.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 17.5, "CB"),
    D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 8.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=own(30), to_go=9)
p.dropback(2.0)
move_to(p, "RB", (-5.6, 1.3), kind="path", speed=2.0)
for k, end in (("WDE", (-5.4, -2.6)), ("WDT", (-4.0, -0.9)), ("SDT", (-4.0, 1.2)), ("SDE", (-5.5, 2.9))):
    move_to(p, k, end, kind="rush")
for k, to, zone in (("LCB", (15.5, -17.0), (8.0, 10.0)), ("FS", (16.0, -6.0), (8.0, 10.5)),
                    ("SS", (16.0, 6.0), (8.0, 10.5)), ("RCB", (15.5, 16.8), (8.0, 10.0)),
                    ("NB", (7.5, -12.5), (5.5, 9.0)), ("WILL", (8.0, -3.5), (5.5, 8.0)),
                    ("MIKE", (8.0, 6.0), (5.5, 9.0))):
    p.drop(k, to, zone=zone)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-22.5, 22.5), window=(-9.5, 22.5), width_in=6.4)
say(f, p, -6.2, -11.0, "4 rush: they must\nwin one-on-one", color=DD, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 20.4, 0.0, "7 in coverage: 4 deep quarters + 3 underneath", color=DD, fontsize=6.9, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -6.6, 7.0, "6 to block 4", color=OD, fontsize=6.6)
field_legend(f.ax, ["rush", "drop", "area"], y=0.0, ncol=3)
plt.show()
```

Why would *not* blitzing be the right plan against the league's best quarterback? Think about what a
blitz gives a quarterback like Mahomes, and what it costs.

- **A blitz trades coverage for speed.** Every extra rusher is one fewer defender in coverage, so somebody
  is uncovered or left one-on-one. A quarterback who reads the blitz before the snap knows where that
  somebody is, and Mahomes was as good as anyone at punishing it with a quick throw or a scramble into the
  space the rushers left.
- **Four plus seven takes away the quick answer.** With seven in coverage, here a quarters shell (four deep, three
  underneath, from [Quarters and Match](../06-pass-coverage/06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd)), every route
  has a defender near it. FTN charted the Eagles in quarters (Cover 4) on `{python} LIX["c4"]` of
  the `{python} LIX["all"]` dropbacks and in two-high coverage of some kind on `{python} LIX["two"]`, far more
  than the `{python} pct(TWOHIGH24_PHI)` two-high rate it charted for them in the regular season. The quarterback has to hold the ball, and every
  half-second he holds it is another half-second for the rush.
- **It only works if four can win.** That is the condition, and it is a roster condition, not a schematic
  one. Jalen Carter, Milton Williams, Jordan Davis, Josh Sweat and Nolan Smith could beat Kansas City's
  blockers one-on-one, on the interior as well as the edges. Most defenses can't get to the quarterback
  rushing four, so they have to blitz.

That last point is the whole chapter in miniature. Fangio's plan was a clever plan, but plenty of
coordinators would have *liked* to rush four and drop seven. Fangio could do it because the front office had
spent first-round picks on Davis (2022), Carter and Smith (2023), had developed Williams from a third-round pick,
and had kept a deep rotation of linemen fresh. The scheme was possible because of the roster.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Super Bowl LIX (February 9, 2025)"}
**The game:** Hurts completed 17 of 22 passes for 221 yards and two touchdowns, ran for 72 yards and scored on
a tush push in the first quarter, and was the game's MVP. DeJean, the rookie, intercepted Mahomes and returned
it 38 yards for a touchdown, on his 22nd birthday. Baun added a second interception before halftime.[^lixbox]

**What to notice:** count the rushers on every Kansas City dropback. You will almost always count four, and
often the same four linemen you saw in their stances, with no linebacker or safety joining them. Then watch
the middle of the pocket. Carter and Williams pushed the interior back toward Mahomes, so he had no room to
step up, and the ends closed in from outside. The pressure came from straight ahead, where a
quarterback can't escape it by drifting sideways.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2022"}
The middle Super Bowl team is the best illustration of the line-first idea working on *both* sides of the
ball. The 2022 Eagles went 14–3. The offense ranked `{python} nth(OFF_RANK[2022])` in EPA per play, with Hurts
the MVP runner-up, Steichen calling plays and the tush push at the start of its run. The defense
recorded `{python} SACKS22` sacks, the most in the league and tied for the third-most by any team in NFL
history, and it was the first team ever with four players reaching double figures.[^sacks22] They lost Super Bowl LVII to Kansas City 38–35, a game
in which Hurts ran for 70 yards and three touchdowns and threw for 304 more.

**What to notice:** on their 2022 film, how often the four-man rush got home by itself. Haason Reddick,
Josh Sweat, Javon Hargrave and Brandon Graham each had at least ten sacks, and the defense rarely needed to
send more. It was the same principle as Fangio's Super Bowl plan, built by a different coordinator
(Jonathan Gannon) two years earlier.
:::

## Roster building: paying for the lines

How did the Eagles keep elite lines for a decade? The tempting answer is "they spent their high draft picks
on linemen," and it is only partly true. From 2013 to 2025 the Eagles spent `{python} int(DRAFT.loc["PHI", "k"])`
of their `{python} int(DRAFT.loc["PHI", "n"])` first- and second-round picks on offensive or defensive
linemen (`{python} pct(DRAFT.loc["PHI", "share"])`), `{python} nth(DRAFT_RANK)` among the 32 franchises
and below the league median of `{python} pct(DRAFT["share"].median())`.[^draft] Their famous lines were built
another way:

1. **Develop the unlikely.** Mailata (seventh round), Kelce (sixth round), Isaac Seumalo (third round) and
   Becton (another team's discarded first-rounder) were turned into starters by Stoutland's coaching. That is
   cheap talent, and a team that can make it has money left for everything else.
2. **Pay to keep them.** When those players became good, the Eagles paid them. Using contract data from Over
   the Cap, the Eagles' offensive line took up `{python} pct(OL_PHI_MEAN, 1)` of the salary cap in an average
   season from 2017 to 2025, against a league median of `{python} pct(OL_MED_MEAN, 1)`, and ranked between
   `{python} nth(OL_RANKS.min())` and `{python} nth(OL_RANKS.max())` in the league every year.[^cap]
3. **Spend the big picks where they move the needle.** The first-round picks of the 2021–2025 drafts went
   to a wide receiver (DeVonta Smith, 2021), two defensive tackles and an edge rusher (Davis, Carter, Nolan Smith),
   a cornerback (Mitchell) and a linebacker (Jihaad Campbell, 2025). Pass rushers who win one-on-one are the scarcest players in football after quarterbacks, and
   you usually can't develop them from the seventh round.
4. **Use the quarterback's cheap years.** In 2022 Hurts was still on his second-round rookie contract, among
   the cheapest starting quarterbacks in the league. That gap between what a good young quarterback earns and
   what a veteran costs is the [rookie-contract window](../14-the-business-of-scheme/14-01-building-a-roster.qmd),
   and the Eagles spent it: they traded for the receiver A.J. Brown and signed Reddick that spring. Hurts's
   five-year, $255 million extension came in April 2023.[^hurts]

Notice how each choice connects to a scheme choice. A team that develops linemen cheaply can afford a
run-first offense, because the line is good enough to win without trickery. A run game that wins with
five blockers frees the quarterback from carrying the offense. A pass rush that wins with four lets the
defensive coordinator play coverage instead of guessing with blitzes. And a sneak that converts every time
the offense needs a yard makes fourth-and-1 a play to run, not a gamble. The roster is the scheme.

The trade-offs are real too. Money spent on linemen is money not spent on receivers or a second
cornerback. Linemen get old together: the Eagles had to replace Kelce, Brooks and Peters within a few seasons
of one another. And an offense whose identity is "our line is better than yours" has a hard time when the
line is merely good, which is one way to read 2025.

## How opponents responded

The league's responses to the Eagles came in three forms.

**On the field.** Defenses attacked the push the only way it can be attacked: by winning the snap. They
crowded both A gaps beside the center with their biggest linemen, timed the cadence so their tackles were
moving as the ball was, and sent linebackers leaping over the pile to meet Hurts before it moved. Some
defensive linemen began jumping the snap count on purpose, accepting an occasional offside penalty for the
chance to get into the backfield first. Against the run game, defenses crowded the box: on first and second
down, the Eagles faced seven or more defenders in the box on `{python} pct(BOX7[2024])` of snaps in 2024 and
`{python} pct(BOX7[2025])` in 2025, when only `{python} int(BOX7_RANK - 1)` offenses saw heavy boxes more often.[^box] (The details of those tactics are in
[Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).)

**In the rulebook.** When you can't stop a play, you can try to ban it. In 2025 Green Bay proposed a rule
against pushing the runner; after being tabled once, a revised version failed 22–10 on May 21, two votes short
of the 24 needed. The league answered by telling its officials to watch more closely for false starts and
players lined up in the neutral zone on the play. In 2026 no team proposed a ban, and the push is legal this
season.[^ban]

**By copying.** The sincerest response was imitation. Other teams, Buffalo most of all, ran sneaks and pushes
in large numbers, and the light-box run game that Philadelphia and others built became one of the league's
standard answers to two-high defenses. And other teams hired the Eagles' coordinators: Steichen to
Indianapolis and Moore to New Orleans as head coaches, and Jonathan Gannon, the 2021–22 defensive
coordinator, to Arizona as head coach in 2023. Success exported the people who had built it, which is the
other cause of the churn.

## What survives

As of the 2026 season, here is where the experiment stands.

- **The head coach and the defense survive.** Sirianni is in his sixth season, and Fangio is still the
  defensive coordinator. The four-man rush philosophy depends on the front office continuing to find
  linemen who can win one-on-one.
- **The quarterback survives.** Hurts, under contract for the long term, is the constant on offense, and
  so is his ability to make the defense account for him as a runner.
- **The architect does not.** Stoutland, the line coach behind every Eagles line since 2013, is gone, and
  the offense has its fifth coordinator in Sirianni's six seasons. The most interesting question for the
  2026 Eagles is whether the trench identity was a *system* that outlives its coach, or a *person*.
- **The push is legal**, but its edge has shrunk. Whether the 2026 Eagles still call it on most of their
  1-yard downs, and whether it still converts at the league's rate when they do, is the cleanest test you
  can run from your couch this season.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Trench check, on any Eagles third- or fourth-and-short:**

- **Before the snap, guess the call.** Hurts under center with two players tight behind him: push. Hurts in
  the shotgun: almost anything but a sneak. Under center with backs at normal depth: a sneak is still possible,
  but so is a handoff or a play-action pass.
- **Count the defense's middle.** How many linemen are in the A gaps beside the center? Is there a linebacker
  standing a couple of yards behind the pile, ready to leap? Did a defensive lineman jump early?
- **Watch the snap, not the pile.** On a push that works, the Eagles' line moves before the defensive linemen
  have risen out of their stances. On one that fails, the defense moved first.
- **Keep a tally.** Calls, conversions, and the distance (inches or a full yard). After a few weeks you will
  have your own version of @fig-sneak-delta, and you will see the selection problem for yourself.
- **On the Eagles' defense, count rushers on passing downs.** Four, with seven in coverage, is the Fangio
  default. A fifth rusher means he thinks the four can't win against this line.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the 2017 RPO"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-rpo
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10, the 2017 Eagles in 11 personnel, shotgun, three receivers to the right. The quarterback will hand off on inside zone or throw a quick screen to H; he decides after the snap."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -17.0, "X"), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 6.6, "Y"),
                 O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 11.5, "H"), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 16.5, "Z")]
dfn = dline() + [D("WILL", "LB", 4.8, -2.4, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.8, 1.6, "M"),
                 D("NB", "NB", 4.4, 5.6, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 16.5, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 9.0, 11.0, "SS"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -17.0, "CB"),
                 D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=own(40), to_go=10)
p.highlight("NB")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-20.0, 20.0), window=(-7.5, 16.5), width_in=6.4)
point_to(f, p, (5.4, 11.2), (4.4, 5.6), "the nickel has walked\ninto the box", color=DD, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**Hand off or throw? Count before you answer.**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Throw the quick screen to H.** Count the right side outside the box: three receivers (Y, H, Z) against two
defenders (the cornerback and the strong safety, who is nine yards deep). The nickel back, who should be the
third man out there, has walked inside to help against the run, making seven in the box against six
blockers. The defense has chosen to stop the handoff with numbers, so the offense throws where the numbers
are in its favour: three receivers against two defenders, with the safety a long way off.

This is exactly the read the RPO hands a quarterback, and it is why the 2017 Eagles leaned on it with Foles:
the defense makes the decision, and the quarterback only has to see it. **What would change it:** if the
nickel had stayed outside over H, the count in the box would be six against six, and the handoff is the
play. The throw and the run are never both bad, which is the point.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: second-and-6, 2024"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-box
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-6, the 2024 Eagles in 11 personnel from the shotgun, Barkley beside Hurts, against a nickel defense with both safeties twelve yards deep."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"),
                 O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -17.5, "X"),
                 O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -10.5, "H"), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 16.5, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.3, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.9, "E"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.8, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.8, 1.4, "M"),
       D("NB", "NB", 4.6, -10.0, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.6, -17.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.6, 16.5, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -7.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 7.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=own(45), to_go=6)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-20.0, 20.0), window=(-7.5, 16.5), width_in=6.4)
say(f, p, 8.4, 0.0, "how many in the box?", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

**What is the most likely call, and why?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A run: duo or zone to Barkley, quite possibly with a throw attached.** Count the box: four linemen and two
linebackers, six defenders. The offense has five linemen and a tight end, six blockers, and Hurts as a
possible runner. Both safeties start twelve yards deep, so the first defender who can arrive unblocked is two
seconds and ten yards away. The defense is playing the pass, and this is the bet the 2024 Eagles punished all
season: they ran on more of their snaps than any other team, mostly against looks like this one.

**What would change it:** a safety walking down toward the line before the snap. Then there are seven in the
box against six blockers, and the better play is a throw behind the safety who left, or a run with Hurts
reading the extra defender.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-9, Super Bowl LIX"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-lix
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-9, Kansas City with three receivers to the right. The Eagles show six players at the line: four linemen and two linebackers walked up into the gaps beside the center, with both safeties deep."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -18.0, "X"), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 6.5, "Y"),
                 O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 11.5, "H"), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 17.5, "Z")]
dfn = dline(w=(-5.0, -2.6, 2.6, 5.2)) + [
    D("WILL", "LB", 2.0, -1.0, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 2.0, 1.0, "M"), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 10.0, "$"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -18.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 17.0, "CB"),
    D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=own(25), to_go=9)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-7.5, 16.5), width_in=6.4)
point_to(f, p, (6.0, -6.4), (2.0, -1.0), "two linebackers in\nthe A gaps", color=DD, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**How many will rush? What is the defense trying to make Mahomes do?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Four.** The two linebackers in the A gaps are there to be *seen*, not to rush. At the snap they back out
into the short middle, and the four linemen rush. Six at the line is a
[pressure look](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd): it makes the offense set its
protection for six, so the center and guards are busy with linebackers who aren't coming, while the four real
rushers may get a one-on-one they wouldn't otherwise see. Behind it, seven defenders cover five receivers.

In the real game this was the Eagles' answer on almost every dropback: by FTN's charting, four or fewer
rushers on `{python} LIX["le4"]` of `{python} LIX["all"]`. **What would change it:** a Fangio defense
blitzes when it doesn't trust four to win. Against a line it can beat, it will show you six and rush four
all night.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- The Eagles' decade is one long bet on the **lines of scrimmage**: elite blockers and pass rushers as the
  stable core, and the quarterback, the coordinator and the scheme around them allowed to change.
- **2017** won with a backup quarterback because RPOs gave him simple reads, the line made the run real, and
  Pederson went for it on fourth down when others kicked. The **Philly Special** worked by exploiting a
  defensive rule (nobody covers the quarterback) at the moment the defense was most committed to the run.
- The **Sirianni-era offense** ran because Hurts made the defense account for an extra runner and the line
  could win both the shoving match of duo and the race of outside zone. That made Barkley's 2,000-yard
  season possible against the league's light boxes. Five offensive coordinators in six seasons show how much
  of that rested on the line rather than the play-caller.
- The **tush push** edge was real but smaller than its reputation, and it faded after 2023. The Eagles converted
  at about the league's rate while running the play far more often, and on harder snaps; the edge was
  **volume without a drop in success**, and by 2025 even that was gone.
- **Super Bowl LIX** was won with a four-man rush and seven in coverage, no blitzes, which is possible only
  for a team whose four linemen can win one-on-one. That scheme was a consequence of draft picks.
- **Roster and scheme are one decision.** Develop linemen cheaply, pay to keep the good ones, spend
  first-round picks on pass rushers, and you can run, sneak and rush four. Everything has a price, and
  the Eagles paid theirs at receiver, at cornerback depth and in the age curve of a veteran line.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From simulation to real tracking data.** The Philly Special animation is a gridiron simulation written in NFL
Big Data Bowl (BDB) coordinates; there is no public tracking data from 2017. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release
(2022 season, weeks 1–9) does cover the Eagles' first big season of tush pushes, ten frames a second before and
after the snap, so you can draw real ones with the same code. The data lives on Kaggle and needs your own free
login, so this cell is not run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
# Eagles quarterback runs on 1 yard to go: the sneaks and pushes of 2022
pushes = plays[(plays["possessionTeam"] == "PHI") & (plays["yardsToGo"] <= 1)
               & plays["playDescription"].str.contains("J.Hurts", na=False)
               & plays["playDescription"].str.contains("up the middle|guard", case=False, na=False)]
print(len(pushes), "candidate pushes")
g, pl = pushes.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[-0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0])
```
